newsitem.title: USA: JAPAN PORK IMPORTS STAY LOW DESPITE FALLING STOCKS. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: JAPAN PORK IMPORTS STAY LOW DESPITE FALLING STOCKS. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]

text.p: Japanese pork imports have remained slow despite a sharp reduction in Japan's pork stocks from last year, and U.S. analysts continue to wonder when Japan will start buying American pork.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Japanese pork stocks at the end of June at only 30 percent of the previous year, while imported stocks were only at 26.2 percent of a year earlier (corrects comparison).

"Sooner or later they have to budge -- they have no choice because their basic consumption pattern isn't changing a whole lot" and stocks are falling, said Dale Durchholz, AgriVisor Services Inc market analyst.

Japan's total pork stocks at the end of June totalled 87,609 tonnes, down from 288,929 tonnes a year earlier. Stocks of imported pork in June totalled 71,478 tonnes, compared to 272,518 tonnes in June 1996.

While monthly total pork demand in Japan has run at an average of 122,000 tonnes in the last year, pork imports in June 1997 fell to only 17,975 tonnes -- 12 percent of the 145,454 tonnes imported in June 1996.

Analysts and pork traders have been looking for Japan to start buying large amounts of U.S. pork since Taiwan, its top pork supplier, banned pork exports in March after an epidemic of foot and mouth disease hit Taiwan's swine herd.
But significant new sales have not occurred. Even with Japan cutting an emergency pork import tariff as of July 1, exports from the U.S. to Japan remain below expectations, analysts said.
Japan's total pork imports in March 1997 were 23,207 tonnes, rising only to 41,974 tonnes in April before falling back to 34,271 tonnes in May.
Meanwhile, Durchholz said, Japan has been working down its pork stocks by some 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes a month.
Durchholz said if July usage was like June's, Japan could have total pork stocks at end-July down to around 60,000 tonnes and at end-August as low as 30,000 tonnes.
But not all analysts were positive Japan would be actively buying large amounts of U.S. pork soon.

Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp in Chicago, said Japan's stocks at the end of June 1995 were 92,889 tonnes and at end-June 1994 were 95,788 tonnes. This puts the June 1997 level down less than 10 percent by comparison.

Also, he said Japan's June 1996 pork stocks were inflated by a burst of imports after removal of a "gate" tariff last year. July 1996 pork imports returned to a more reasonable level of 40,760 tonnes.
Levitt said Japan's supply of pork in storage now, although historically low, is in line with previous years.

"Even though it looks like they have nothing versus a year ago, last year was inflated sustantially when they lifted the safeguard mechanism in the spring of last year. The imports of pork just exploded and led to a huge stock buildup," Levitt said.
But he added that he does expect Japan to step up pork imports in the next couple of months. The country needs to start building up its stock base, Levitt said.

One factor slowing Japan's imports below expectations has been exchange rates. The weakening of the yen against the dollar for most of this year helped raise the price of imported pork to a level that reduced domestic demand, analysts said.
The yen has recovered slightly against the dollar since May.
A sharp rise in domestic pork prices may have also trimmed retail demand and shifted consumer buying to other meat items, they said.
